title: What happens if the outbox relay/publisher sends an event to Kafka and then crashes BEFORE marking the outbox row as published — the event can be sent again when the publisher resumes, which is expected in an at-least-once design — and why does this mean downstream consumers MUST be idempotent (they may receive the same event more than once), and how do you prevent the outbox table from growing unboundedly (periodic cleanup of published rows, retention policy)?
shortTitle: What happens if the outbox relay crashes BEFORE marking the row published, why must consumers be idempotent, and how do you stop the outbox table growing unboundedly?

s1_definition.profdef: In an outbox-plus-relay design, the relay reads an unpublished outbox row, publishes it to Kafka, and then marks the row published. These are two separate steps against two systems, so if the relay crashes between the Kafka send and the mark, the row stays unpublished and the relay re-sends it on restart. This is at-least-once delivery: every event is delivered one or more times, never zero. Because duplicates are inevitable, downstream consumers must be idempotent — processing the same event twice must have the same effect as processing it once. Separately, published outbox rows must be purged by a retention job or the table grows forever.
s1_definition.analogy: The messenger at National Bank of India opens the outbox drawer, grabs a transfer slip, hands it to the Kafka courier, and is supposed to then stamp the slip "SENT" in the drawer. One day the messenger handed over Rajesh's slip and fainted before stamping it. When he woke up, the slip still looked unsent, so he handed it to the courier again — now two identical slips are in transit. That is fine as long as the receiving departments are smart: when the Notification desk gets a slip it has already seen (same slip number), it throws the duplicate away instead of texting Rajesh twice. And because the drawer fills up, a clerk comes every night and shreds all the slips already stamped "SENT" so the drawer never overflows.
s1_definition.oneliner: At-least-once means send-then-mark can produce duplicates, so consumers must deduplicate by event id, and a retention job must delete published rows so the outbox never grows without bound.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** In an outbox-plus-relay design, the relay reads an unpublished outbox row, publishes it to Kafka, and then marks the row published. These are two separate steps against two systems, so if the relay crashes between the Kafka send and the mark, the row stays unpublished and the relay re-sends it on restart. This is at-least-once delivery: every event is delivered one or more times, never zero. Because duplicates are inevitable, downstream consumers must be idempotent — processing the same event twice must have the same effect as processing it once. Separately, published outbox rows must be purged by a retention job or the table grows forever.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The messenger at National Bank of India opens the outbox drawer, grabs a transfer slip, hands it to the Kafka courier, and is supposed to then stamp the slip "SENT" in the drawer. One day the messenger handed over Rajesh's slip and fainted before stamping it. When he woke up, the slip still looked unsent, so he handed it to the courier again — now two identical slips are in transit. That is fine as long as the receiving departments are smart: when the Notification desk gets a slip it has already seen (same slip number), it throws the duplicate away instead of texting Rajesh twice. And because the drawer fills up, a clerk comes every night and shreds all the slips already stamped "SENT" so the drawer never overflows.

**One line to remember:** At-least-once means send-then-mark can produce duplicates, so consumers must deduplicate by event id, and a retention job must delete published rows so the outbox never grows without bound.

sections.s2_technical:
The relay does three things in order: it selects unpublished rows, it publishes each to Kafka, and it marks each published. Marking published and publishing to Kafka are two different systems — a database update and a broker send — so there is no atomic way to do both. If the relay crashes after the Kafka send but before the database mark, the row remains flagged unpublished. On restart the relay re-selects it and publishes it again. This is deliberate. The design chooses at-least-once over at-most-once because losing a banking event (a transfer that no one is notified about) is far worse than delivering it twice.

Why not mark first, then send? Then a crash after marking but before sending would lose the event entirely — at-most-once, which is unacceptable for money. So we always send first and mark second, accepting duplicates.

Because duplicates are guaranteed, idempotency is not optional for consumers. Idempotent means that applying the same operation multiple times leaves the same result as applying it once. There are several ways a consumer achieves this. The simplest is a processed-events table: the consumer records the event id it has handled, and at the start of processing it checks `if (processedRepo.existsById(eventId)) return;`. A code example is `if (processedRepo.exists(event.getId())) { log.info("duplicate skipped"); return; } process(event); processedRepo.save(event.getId());`. Another way is natural idempotency — if the operation is "set balance to X" rather than "add X to balance", repeating it is harmless. A third way is an upsert keyed by a business id so a repeated insert becomes a no-op update. A fourth is a unique database constraint on the event id that makes the second insert throw, which the consumer swallows.

A subtle point: the dedup check and the business write should themselves be in one transaction, or you can get a crash between "wrote the business change" and "recorded the event id as processed", which would re-process. Recording the processed id in the same transaction as the business effect closes that gap.

Now the retention problem. Every committed transfer inserts an outbox row. If you never delete published rows, the table grows forever, slowing down the relay's "find unpublished" query (even with a partial index), bloating backups, and eventually filling disk. The fix is a retention policy: a scheduled job deletes rows where published is true and created_at is older than some window, for example `DELETE FROM outbox WHERE published = TRUE AND created_at < now() - INTERVAL '7 days'`. The window exists so operators can still inspect recently published events for debugging. For very high volume, partitioning the outbox table by day and dropping whole old partitions is cheaper than row-by-row deletes. If you use Debezium CDC, you can even configure it so that after routing a row it deletes it, keeping the table tiny.

A senior nuance: deletes should be batched and throttled (delete 10,000 rows at a time with a short pause) so the cleanup job does not hold long locks or spike I/O during business hours. Another nuance is monitoring — alert if the count of unpublished rows (the relay backlog) grows, because that means the relay or Kafka is stuck and events are piling up.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India the Transfer Service writes TransferCompleted events to an outbox, and a relay ships them to Kafka where the Notification Service consumes them to text customers.

Problem 1 — The fainting messenger. The relay published Rajesh's TransferCompleted to Kafka, then the pod was killed by a rolling deploy before it could mark the row. On restart it re-published the same event. The Notification Service texted Rajesh twice: "50,000 debited" appeared on his phone twice and he called support confused. This is exactly at-least-once delivery producing a duplicate, and the Notification Service was not idempotent.

Problem 2 — The overflowing drawer. After a year, the outbox table had 400 million rows, all long since published. The relay's "find unpublished" scan slowed, nightly backups ballooned, and disk alerts fired. This is the unbounded-growth problem — published rows were never cleaned up.

The fix has two parts. First, make the consumer idempotent by tracking processed event ids and skipping duplicates. Second, run a retention job that deletes published rows older than the retention window.

The code will have an `OutboxEvent`, an `OutboxRepository`, an `OutboxRelay` that can crash between send and mark, a `NotificationConsumer` with a `ProcessedEventRepository` for idempotency, and a `RetentionJob` that purges old published rows. The demo publishes once, simulates a crash so the event is sent twice, shows the consumer skipping the duplicate, then runs retention and shows the table shrink.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: one outbox row, TransferCompleted for Rajesh's 50,000 transfer.

Step 1 — The relay selects the unpublished row and sends it to Kafka. The consumer receives event id E1, sees it is new, sends the SMS, and records E1 as processed.

Step 2 — The relay crashes before marking the row published. The row still looks unpublished.

Step 3 — The relay restarts and selects the same row again (it was never marked). It sends event id E1 to Kafka a second time. This is the at-least-once duplicate.

Step 4 — The consumer receives E1 again, checks its processed-events table, finds E1 already there, and skips — no second SMS. Idempotency saved Rajesh from a confusing duplicate text.

Step 5 — The relay now marks the row published. The data in the outbox flips from unpublished to published.

Step 6 — Days later the row is 10 days old and published. The retention job runs, finds it older than the 7-day window, and deletes it. The outbox shrinks, keeping the relay query fast and disk usage bounded.

sections.s6_takeaway:
In an outbox design the relay reads an unpublished row, publishes it to Kafka, and then marks the row published. Those last two steps hit two different systems, so there is no way to make them atomic. If the relay crashes after the Kafka send but before the database mark, the row stays unpublished and the relay re-sends it on restart. We deliberately order it send-first, mark-second, because if we marked first and then crashed before sending we would lose the event entirely, and silently losing a banking event is far worse than delivering it twice. That ordering is what makes the design at-least-once.

The direct consequence is that duplicates are guaranteed, so downstream consumers must be idempotent, meaning processing the same event twice has the same effect as processing it once. In my banking notification service I kept a processed-events table keyed by the event id; at the start of handling an event I check whether that id is already recorded, skip it if so, and otherwise send the SMS and record the id in the same transaction as the business effect. I also committed the Kafka offset only after that idempotent processing, so a crash just replays the event rather than skipping it.

The second problem is that every committed transfer inserts an outbox row, so if I never clean up, the table grows without bound, the relay's find-unpublished query slows down, backups bloat, and disk eventually fills. I solved this with a retention policy: a scheduled job deletes rows that are both published and older than a window such as seven days, keeping recent events available for debugging. For high volume I partitioned the outbox table by day and dropped whole old partitions, which is far cheaper than row-by-row deletes, and I batched and throttled any deletes to avoid long locks during business hours.

The deeper principle I always state is that at-least-once delivery pushes the correctness responsibility onto the consumer: the broker and relay promise to deliver at least once, and the consumer promises to be idempotent, and together those two promises give you effectively exactly-once business behavior without needing an impossible distributed atomic commit.

The one-line summary I give is: send-then-mark makes the relay re-send on crash, so consumers must deduplicate by event id, and a retention job must delete published rows so the outbox stays bounded.
